cards.title: New Evidence Shows School Phone Bans Are Gradually Improving Test Scores

depth.text: a study links **school phone bans** to a **small test-score bump**, though commenters question what caused it

One commenter says the study found a **≈0.01 standard-deviation difference** in test scores in the year lockable phone pouches were adopted, with **no detectable additional difference** the following year. Critics point to diverging pre-trends and ask whether post-COVID recovery explains the gains.

cards.camps: Two camps: ban supporters say students socialize more and phones should have been banned sooner; skeptics say score gains are small or may reflect other factors.

cards.title: Apple Services Down

depth.text: Apple services went **down**, and users reported trouble **signing in** and using everyday features

One commenter said an Apple Store couldn't process **orders or returns**, and newly bought iPhones couldn't be **activated**. Others reported **Apple Account sign-in errors**; a linked report also mentioned problems with Apple Pay and the App Store.

cards.camps: Two camps: some wonder about a coordinated attack or AWS; others point to operational strain, rushed updates, or long-neglected infrastructure.

comments.text: This reminds me of the Chinese spy balloon that floated over the US. For a week or so we were getting news stories about every unidentified weather balloon or piece of airborne debris. The main connection between the incidents was that the public thought they might be connected.
Just got back from the Apple Store. They confirmed that everything was down, they could not process orders or returns, and new iPhones that people bought weren't able to be activated.

what a world we built in less than a generation... everything and everyone dependent on a few cloud services, we're very far from the original vision of a decentralised internet :'( The only chance we have for a more reliable world is if these outages and hacks become more and more common. Institutions and people will be forced to wake up and find more local and diverse alternatives...

TIL Apple has two status pages: https://developer.apple.com/system-status/ https://www.apple.com/support/systemstatus/ Interesting that HomeKit makes the general status page and not the developer one. Makes me wonder how they define each entry, and what makes up a system in one vs. the other.
Well this has been an interesting week.

cards.title: We don't need more apps, we need better open source

depth.text: someone wants **AI coding** aimed at making **open-source tools** easier to run, not building more apps

Krueger points to **uv**, whose makers’ benchmarks say it installs Python packages **8 to 10 times faster than pip** (up to 115 times with a warm cache). He says AI can help profile code, write tests, test installers and write docs, but **a person checks every line**.

cards.camps: Two camps: some want AI improving shared open-source projects; others prefer custom apps for individual needs, while maintainers warn that extra fixes can overwhelm them.

comments.text: > Pick one open source tool you use. Find the most annoying thing about installing or running it. Spend a weekend fixing it, with the people who maintain it. Then tell me about it. My open source projects were barely sustainable when the few PRs that came in would fix actual, non-hypothetical, serious logic problems. Now I've been seeing PRs like that, fixing annoyances, performance edge cases…

I think we need a new model of software delivery. Here's my most-recent real-world problem: I wanted to plug in my midi controller keyboard and just play a piano, so I can practice my choral music. > Pick one open source tool you use. [...] Spend a weekend fixing it Beware: Your best path forward there may be, contrary to part of the thesis in this post, be to vibe code a replacement. For example, I've had bug fixes to significant problems be rejected because "we are in the future going to be…

I just tell it what I ate two or three times per day, voice or text, no attempt to normalize units or food names. It does all of that with nuance and I seldom have to correct anything…

cards.title: What is the best harness for each model?

depth.text: someone tested coding setups and found the **best-value harness** changes with each **model**

The team compared **22 harnesses** across **five models**, on 62 terminal tasks with four attempts each. “Best value” meant the **lowest cost per pass**, unless another option cost at most 30% more per pass and passed at least five points more often. Picks included Codex CLI with GLM-5.3, Pi with GLM-5.3 Flash, ZCode with DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017, Oh My Pi with Muse, and Alma with Kimi-K3.

cards.camps: Two camps: some say a harness barely changes results for a fixed model; others say a task-specific harness can be much faster, cheaper, and more correct.

comments.text: The headline here is confusing. They ran a bunch of harness and agent combinations on terminal bench tasks, and 64% of the spending was on tasks that didn’t pass terminal bench verifiers. It’s unclear whether that’s supposed to be surprising against the selected models for the benchmark. I suspect it’s not and the headline is written to pander to “wasting money on AI” upvotes. Edit: they changed…

I find myself pulled in two directions by the performance of coding agents: First, keeping them on a short leash seems sensible. I don't get failed results very often. When I first started using coding agents, this seemed not just sensible but required in order to not deal with a lot of hallucinated weirdness. Secondly though, it's pretty cool to vaguely wave your hands in a certain direction and…

As someone who regularly uses Claude Opus 5.5 from Claude Code and from Copilot, I would say harness barely matters in terms overall performance and behavior. Opus is nearly identical in both harness. The opposite is also true, if I switch Copilot to something like Gemini 4 Argon it's completely…

I don't like this framing. For a given model, the best harness depends on the problem. As models become increasingly capable, the harness appears to matter more than the model. This is perhaps controversial but allow me to explain. Most of my problems are in a single domain, using specific tools and programming languages. I give whatever model de jour the specific tools it needs to solve the…

However, I am hesitant on the correlation between pass/fail in evals which are a binary 0/1 determined by tests, and real world usage, where users can steer, run code review, and care about more than just test pass/fail. cards.title: Why 3dfx 1 cards had such a washed out color output?

depth.text: John Carmack explains why **textures made for ordinary screens** looked **washed out** on 3DFX cards

Carmack says 3DFX used near-linear color with only **5 or 6 bits per channel**, which could cause bands in dark colors; textures made for conventional non-linear displays then looked **washed out**. A commenter says some cards also had **signal-voltage** differences that gamma adjustment would not fix.

cards.camps: Two takes: Carmack points to color-space and texture mismatch; a commenter says signal-voltage problems—not gamma—also affected some cards.

comments.text: I have two alternate observations, because VGA is an analog signal there are standards for what the voltages should be. But they were not always followed. Keep in mind that the first two Voodoo cards were also video switchers with a chip to output either the 2D passthrough or the internally generated 3D chip signal created by its own GENDAC. 1. I have a Voodoo 2 paired with an S3 Virge/DX, the…

One other aspect of 3dfx looking a bit washed out beyond the gamma problem is the trickery performed in the RAMDAC before it blasted those cool pixels to the VGA port. If you remember, 3dfx screenshots were just as dithered as, say, an ATI Rage, but on screen it looked smoother (although a bit blurry) while the others looked visibly dithered still (see some 3dfx screenshots…
It's pretty cool that someone can ask an interesting graphics-related question, and John Carmack of all people steps in to answer it. And then even Eric S. Raymond adds a comment further below.

You might have heard about sRGB (the commonly used colorspace) not being linear, and that to get halfway between black and white (linear RGB of 50%), you get an sRGB value of around 74%. But there is one place where sRGB is truly linear, and that is signal voltage for a CRT display . 50% of sRGB truly means 50% of signal voltage (between the minimum and maximum voltages).

Hard to believe, but Nvidia, founded by former SGI engineers, was considered an entrepreneur and challenger of 3dfx, the dominant pioneer in PC 3D hardware 30 years ago. Edit: see comments re founders

cards.title: Comcast's "fiber-powered Wi-Fi" is cable, AT&T says in false advertising case

depth.text: AT&T says Comcast’s **fiber-powered Wi-Fi** claim describes cable service that reaches homes over **coaxial cable**

The lawsuit asks for Comcast’s **profits from the ads** and a **permanent injunction** against the phrase. AT&T has an awkward history too: an ad watchdog said its old **“5GE”** label for 4G LTE could mislead customers.

cards.camps: Two camps: some say coax isn’t fiber and fiber has practical advantages; others say users care about bandwidth and availability, and cable can be symmetric.

comments.text: Fiber is so much better than cable in an emergency. The equipment consumes significantly less power and is likely to stay up longer during a power outage. You get way more customers on each battery / generator. I had an FTTH provider with 100% of their network on natural gas standby generators. Went through a week long power outage without losing a single packet. You can support something like…

While Comcast has deployed plenty of fiber throughout the US, its cable Internet service makes the final connection to homes with coaxial cable. This results in upload speeds being far slower than download speeds. In contrast, fiber-to-the-home service can provide symmetrical upload and download speeds. You can get symmetric DOCSIS, and apparently Comcast do offer that service[1]. Likewise, FTTH…

Back in the days of rolling out U-Verse (their FTTN service), AT&T's advertising used exactly the same strategy of weasel-words to say "fiber" without making an actionable implication that it was fiber from A to Z. Phrases like "fiber rich network" and "U-Verse uses fiber optic technology."

This has been a thing in the Netherlands for years. Ziggo has been advertising with terms like "Glasvezel-Kabel" (Fiber Optic - Cable) to indicate that the fiber goes up to a switch in the area, but then goes over coax cable to the residential buildings. They got a lawsuit, and for some weird reason they even won it. I don't know it it really matters in the end, they lose some (technical)…
The advertising in this space is terrible. I constantly see ads for "gig wifi" and similar terms and have no idea what the actual internet connection type is.

cards.title: If an App Asks for Full Disk Access or System and App Protection Override

depth.text: Mac users can give apps **limited access** to folders or apps instead of letting them **bypass protections**

Full Disk Access lets an app **read, change, delete, and export** every file on your Mac. System & App Protection Override can also let it control your Mac, see background windows, and **capture every keystroke**; you can change either permission later in Privacy & Security settings.

cards.camps: Two camps: supporters say choosing limited access is a useful safety step; critics say Apple's design is clumsy and doesn't give developers enough precise permission controls.

comments.text: This is a very poorly conceived API. If developers' use cases don't fit cleanly into Apple's (narrow) idea about how a hypothetical app should work, developers will continue to feel like they need to request these expansive permissions. A good filesystem permission API could include any of these which would make users WAY safer and enable developers to request far smaller scopes: - Allow the…

This is a good thing. There are too many apps that request full disk access despite not needing it. I counted 44* applications on my mac that ask for FDA. I've only granted it to 8. The other apps work just fine without it. (Some apps that ask for full disk access: Anki, a flashcard app and Soulver, a calculator app – cmon now) This change is less about bureaucracy and more requiring developers…

For me more important would be to exclude specific folders from that full disk access (like ~/.ssh), rather than selecting one directory. For example I've used Daisy Disk app to visualize directory size. It's best used with full disk access. But I know that my `.ssh` is tiny and I'd prefer for this app not to be able to access it at all.

I think Apple is being smart here and people are blowing this way out of proportion for views. The truth is that we've seen people who know how to run secops get hacked, so putting controls to ensure we scare the shit out of people who think giving claude access to their entire disk is no big deal is a great idea.
This seems like a fine change? I don’t quite understand what the pushback is could someone spell it out for me?

cards.title: How the Claude Code team thinks about verification

depth.text: the Claude Code team shares how **feedback loops** help coding agents **check their own work**
They recommend **end-to-end tests** first, plus **property tests** that try thousands of inputs to catch edge cases. If a check still fails after three rounds, Claude stops and **brings in a human**.

cards.camps: Two camps: skeptics say these checks add cost or unnecessary process; supporters say a strong QA workflow improves trust and helps them ship quality software.

comments.text: This article feels like the result of having unlimited tokens at your disposal. It’s got some very expensive practices, where near-free practices would produce the same or better results. There’s a long section in the middle where the article describes per-change verification via skill files and “ask Claude to use the chrome-for-Claude tool” when checking if changes have introduced regressions…

Is Claude Code considered to be a reliable piece of software these days? I stopped using as my daily driver around 9 months ago, and at that time it felt very heavy/janky and seemed to have very regular bugs and breaking UI changes. I’d be happy to hear that it has gotten better!
The Claude code team doesn’t think about jack sh*t. Interacting with Anthropic teams makes it clear that nobody at that company has any idea how their software works.
> With them, you can run dozens or hundreds in parallel. Im already spending my $2k usd per month in tokens with just one or two agents. How do they expect me to do that?

> Nobody can read every change, so we use failures as one way to decide what needs a person. Whether a human can or should review every diff is a conscious project level decision. I have yet to see a project where it is not feasible. The trick is to break things into small enough pieces that you can review them. Just like one would do if you were doing such changes manually. Nobody in their right…

cards.title: VisualBasic.World: A gallery of Planet Source Code programs from 1997 to 2012

depth.text: someone made a **gallery** of old Visual Basic projects that feels like a **time capsule**

comments.text: A lovely gaggle of whacky, strange, and absolutely diverse projects. Very of the era with some of them. Views like this being me joy because it shows a more raw view of people just playing with technology and figuring it out rather than everything having to be perfect. With AI powered project cleanup it will be hard to land back into a phase like this. Feels like everything lands in sort of a…

What a fun scroll. VB6 also brings back a lot of memories for me. I remember using Visual C++6 to learn DirectX8, but didn't know about DLLs, so I rewrote every single C++ function in VB6 to create my level editor. Never went anywhere though. Also: Lexx Solitaire [1] - today's thing I discovered that I didn't know I needed! [1] https://github.com/Planet-Source-Code/erling-andersen-lexx-s...

VB5 had the hands down best development IDE IMHO. You could rewrite code in debug mode and highlight anything and hit F1 for context help. Creating a client server application using DCOM and watching the client call the server in debug mode was cool. In 1997 a VB5/MS-SQL Server job listed in the paper was my first programming gig.

Learned programming on VB 5/6 by doing drag and drop on windows with controls and copying basic code from a book. I made myself little “homework helper” programs and also “annoyatron” apps to install on friends computers by floppy. Tricks like hiding a window but keeping the program resident or in the system tray occupied my mind. Spent hours at a time trying out various custom controls. Good…

I used to love Planet Source Code. I submitted quite a few projects there. They used to have a prize for the highest rated project each month and I won that a few times too. It also helped kick start my development in DirectX. I don’t think I used PSC much after around 2002. By that point I’d migrated to Linux as my primary OS and PSC was largely more a Windows audience back then.

cards.title: MAI Code 2 and Code 2 Flash

depth.text: Microsoft launched **two coding models**, one for **common enterprise work** and one for **routine high-volume tasks**

Across four benchmarks, Microsoft says MAI Code 2 reaches **98% of GPT 6.1 Sol’s performance** at **40% of the cost**. Both models are **available in GitHub Copilot**, though Microsoft says comparisons vary by workload and pricing assumptions.

cards.camps: Two camps: some praise the comparisons with leading models; others discount launch benchmarks and question whether the price advantage holds.

comments.text: I'd hate to be OpenAI and Anthropic. They are better than the rest of the available models currently, but only by a few months. That is a very tenuous lead and doesn't speak to much of a sustainable competitive moat for either company. The have to keep sprinting as fast as possible on the hamster wheel to just stay ahead.

Probably would be a good time to rename it “Mai” (like the name) instead of the corporate “MAI” if they’re gonna be serious players. I don’t think any research has really been done into this, but in my anecdotal usage a coherent persona seems to help the models achieve more. Even Qwen seems to perform better when I talk to it as Qwen instead of generically.

If these benchmarks can hold up in real life, we are seeing again and again an intelligence explosion in front of our eyes and devaluation of intelligence. Anyone has more background how they were able to catch up that fast? Distillation of GPT due to their OpenAI acess to the model might make most sense but they probably are not allowed to do that.

I wish they would've talked more about the visual coding. The fact that the visuals this produces is preferable to 6.1 Sol over 60% of the time is heartening, but I would've loved to see them go against Opus 5.5 which as far as I can tell is the king for UIs at this price point.

I really hope they keep writing technical reports even as their models get better. MAI-Thinking-1 is far more in depth than anything else recent I could find, and very valuable to those outside the labs.

cards.title: Nimony: A New Compiler for Nim

depth.text: someone built a **new compiler** for Nim, bringing **borrow checking** and **sum types**

Nimony is the home of Nim 3, with **native code generation** for x86_64, ARM64, ARM32, AVR and RISC-V. The same code base compiles to C, native code, JavaScript and WebAssembly, and an index that is provably out of range can trigger a **compile-time error**.

comments.text: When I was doing the rounds roughly 10 years ago, trying to find a new programming language to learn, my money for "next big thing" landed on nim. I did some personal projects and absolutely loved it but, unfortunately, opportunities to work "on the clock" in nim never materialised and then rust started eating the world. Thanks, Andreas Rumpf, for sticking with it for all these years: This seems…

I’m curious if this closes the door on Nim’s capability to output C code which you then compile yourself. I first discovered Nim when I was looking for something that could work with Apple’s requirements to embed bitcode in iOS apps, it meant you had to use their specific version of LLVM and that ruled out a lot of languages. It always seemed like a really unique feature (though IIRC Haxe has…

> Nimony is case sensitive like most other modern programming languages. The reason for this is implementation simplicity. This might also be changed in the future. I've never been too annoyed by Nim's approach but I think this removes a complaint many people have.
It’s super exciting. It’s basically adding all the features I wished Nim had, and I’ve been using Nim in anger since the v0.10 days!
This is great! Congrats to the Nim team for keeping the pedal to the metal! Sum-types, borrow-checking... Nim 3 is beautiful.

cards.title: Loopholes Are for Assholes

depth.text: someone says **parking wherever you like** isn't clever if everyone else has to **follow the rules**

**Garrity’s test** is to ask what would happen if everyone acted the same way; he applies it to parking in front of Walmart’s doors. Commenters split: some say **consistent loophole use** makes you an asshole, while others say loopholes can expose **badly designed rules**.

cards.title: Windows 11 Is Collecting Data on Which Coding Agents and Developer Tools You Use

depth.text: Windows can **report** which **coding agents and developer tools** you’ve used if optional diagnostics are on

cards.title: Chemistry is Actually Geometry

depth.text: someone uses **geometry** to show how chemical reactions can **settle down** or **keep cycling**

The essay represents each reaction with a **reaction vector** and uses network structure to reason about **equilibria** and oscillations. It works toward the **deficiency zero theorem**, which can bound how many equilibrium points a network has using its structure and geometry.

cards.camps: Two camps: some find the geometric view elegant for picturing reaction dynamics; others say the title oversells its scope or mistakes a useful map for reality.
entities: Foundations of Chemical Reaction Network Theory

comments.text: This post did not go in the direction I expected. From the title I thought the post would explore how chemical reactions depend on the geometry of molecules and the distribution of electrons, but instead it delved into how chemical kinetics can be graphed geometrically.

Reading this, it seems they're using the term "geometry" in a more abstract sense. Pretty much you can turn a reaction's state into an abstract point, and then you can plot that reaction point over time. It becomes concrete again when they plot the path of the reaction's "coordinates" and you can visually see what happened with the reaction. It's quite elegant! Like you can see a system oscillate…

I do not question the author's expertise, and I find the post very interesting; however, we really ought to stop mistaking the map for the territory. While drawing such analogies is certainly very useful and powerful, assuming that this represents reality is truly a stretch, as none of it can be proven. Also I find it a bit pedantic on the "theory" word, giving me the impression that the author…

I worked in a lab where a geologist was taking soundings to understand the geometry of plate techtonics. Smart guy but needed a geek for the Sun server, so I got to ride along. Anyway, lots of things are "actually geometry" but chemistry is kind of the one science that really does just reduce to QED first principles pretty cleanly. You don't hear a lot of talk about emergent chemical phenomena…

Probably a lot of material science is understanding how the molecules are structured in various shapes, crystals, etc. For example, this video shows cool visualizations: What comes after lithium-ion batteries? - https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=huMZI_7iZKA Proteins fold, thats also geometry.

cards.title: Squircles

depth.text: someone breaks down what makes **squircles** different from rounded rectangles and how to **draw** them

A **squircle** sits between a square and a circle, and there isn’t **one standard curve** for it. The post compares **superellipses**, Apple’s flat-sided shape, Figma’s approximation, and CSS’s corner-shape property; it says an exponent of 3 with a matching flat side comes closer to Apple than the old exponent-5 guess.

cards.camps: Two camps: some like squircles as a design shape; others find the icons ugly and miss distinctive app shapes.

comments.text: One of my favorite squircles in the wild was on the Zune 2nd gen models. It felt great to flick through your music, with the added benefit of also being able to click like a regular dpad. It felt smooth, almost like a mini touchpad for your mp3s, but without the cursor.

I'm working on a tool to author better splines and superellipses/clothoids feature heavily. If anyone is interested here's a little demo you can play around with: https://thiic.cc/omnispline/ It's just a giant stack of edge case exceptions that mostly does the thing you'd expect it to, sorry about the UI, it's very much just in the exploration stage.
Squircles are an excellent shape, slightly outdone in my opinion by their dimensional older brother the sphube. Both thoroughly described here: https://arxiv.org/abs/1604.02174

Generally speaking curves that avoid having discontinuities in their derivatives become hugely interesting the moment you want to interact with physical reality, since they are what enable smoothness. Squircles are just part of this.

This is the kind of wholesome content HN needs more of. Some hate it, some love it. My perspective on this post is, great! Another idea I can add to my bookmarks for when I’m designing. Appreciate the OP!

glossary.standard deviation: A yardstick for how spread out results are, used to compare score differences on a common scale.
glossary.pre-trends: Changes happening before a policy starts; different earlier patterns can make it harder to tell what the policy changed.
glossary.diff-in-diff: A way of comparing how two groups change over time to estimate whether a policy made a difference.
glossary.benchmark: A test people use to compare how well different tools do a task.
glossary.Goodhart's Law: The idea that once a measurement becomes a goal, people may optimize for the score instead of what it was meant to measure.
glossary.Pareto frontier: A set of choices where you can't get better on one measure without giving something up on another.
glossary.chain of thought (CoT): The steps an AI appears to use to reach an answer, which people may try to inspect or monitor.
glossary.cloud service: A feature you use over the internet that runs on computers managed by someone else.
glossary.DAV: Distributed Authoring and Versioning: a way for apps to access and update information stored by another service.
glossary.self-host: Run a service on computers you manage yourself.
glossary.AWS: Amazon Web Services: a collection of cloud services run by Amazon.
glossary.open source: Software whose code is shared so other people can inspect, run, or change it.
glossary.vibecoding: Using AI to make software from requests instead of writing each line yourself.
glossary.maintainer: Someone who keeps a software project working and up to date.
glossary.pull request: A proposal to add your code changes to a shared project, usually asking others to review them first.
glossary.warm cache: Information saved from an earlier run, so a later run can skip some work.
glossary.Baader–Meinhof phenomenon: The feeling that something you just learned about suddenly seems to turn up everywhere.
glossary.RCE: Remote Code Execution: a flaw that lets an attacker make a computer run their commands from somewhere else.
glossary.harness: The surrounding code that gives an AI agent tools and a place to work, and checks what it does.
glossary.pass rate: The share of tested tasks that meet the success checks.
glossary.cost per pass: The average spend per task divided by the share of tasks that pass; it estimates the cost of getting a passing result.
glossary.tokens: Small pieces of text an AI counts as it reads or writes; they can affect how much a request costs.
glossary.gamma: A curve that changes how a pixel’s number maps to the brightness you see.
glossary.linear color: A way of representing light where doubling a number means doubling the light.
glossary.bits per channel: How many different steps each color can take; fewer steps can make shades look banded.
glossary.signal voltage: The strength of the electrical signal a card sends to a screen, which can affect how bright the picture looks.
glossary.sRGB: Standard Red Green Blue: a common set of rules for representing screen colors.
glossary.coaxial cable: A wire like the one used for cable TV that can carry internet into a home.
glossary.fiber-to-the-home: An internet connection where fiber-optic cable runs all the way to the home.

glossary.symmetrical speeds: Upload and download speeds that are the same.

glossary.differential test: A test that gives the same input to an old and a new system and checks whether their results differ.
glossary.verification loop: A cycle where an agent runs checks, sees what failed, and uses the results to improve its work.

glossary.SSGI: Screen-Space Global Illumination: An estimate of bounced light made from the scene visible to the camera.
glossary.BRDF: Bidirectional Reflectance Distribution Function: A description of how a material reflects light from different directions.
glossary.CSS: Cascading Style Sheets: rules that control how a web page looks.
glossary.HTML: HyperText Markup Language: code that tells a browser what content a web page has.
glossary.JavaScript: A programming language; here, it lets an agent combine tool calls.
glossary.popover: A browser feature for showing a small panel, like a menu, over a page.
glossary.CSP: Content Security Policy: rules a site gives a browser about which scripts and connections to allow.
glossary.progressive enhancement: Building a website so its basic parts work first, then adding extras for browsers that can handle them.
glossary.server-rendered: When a website sends a page already put together, instead of building it in your browser.
glossary.V8-isolates: Separate, restricted environments for running JavaScript, keeping one task apart from another.
glossary.gzipped: Compressed in a way that makes a file smaller to send or store.
glossary.courseware: Online lessons and activities for taking a class, beyond just watching lectures.
glossary.ETW: Event Tracing for Windows: a Windows system that carries reports about what software is doing.
glossary.bitset: A compact row of yes-or-no bits used to test whether a value belongs to a set.
glossary.DiagTrack: Connected User Experiences and Telemetry: the Windows service that handled the diagnostic report and its upload queue in this investigation.
glossary.WSL: Windows Subsystem for Linux: a way to use Linux tools on Windows.
glossary.UX: User experience: how using a product feels and how easy it is to get things done.
glossary.PageRank: A score Google used to judge how important a web page seemed based on links pointing to it.
glossary.affiliate programs: Deals where a website earns money for sending customers to a retailer.
glossary.Project JavaScript: A place in an Optimizely project where a customer can add code that runs on their pages.
glossary.CDN: Content Delivery Network: A network of servers that helps websites handle requests closer to their users.
glossary.card skimming: Secretly capturing card details entered on a website and sending them to an attacker.
glossary.Subresource Integrity: A browser check that makes sure a downloaded script has not been changed.
glossary.exploit kit: A package of code attackers can use to try exploiting a weakness.
glossary.sum type: A kind of value that can be one of several distinct options, with each option able to carry its own details.
glossary.enum: A named set of possible choices for a value, where each choice can carry different data.
glossary.ownership: A rule for which part of a program is responsible for data and who may change it.
glossary.arena: A reserved chunk of memory for related things that a program can keep around or clear as a group.
glossary.interface: The names and details other code can use from a crate, without needing its inner workings.
glossary.macro: A tool that lets programmers add language features or transform code before it runs.
glossary.weight and balance: A check of how a plane’s load is distributed and how heavy it is before a flight.
glossary.change freeze: A period when teams pause software changes to avoid introducing problems.
glossary.LLMs: Large language models: computer programs trained on lots of writing that can produce text.
glossary.firmware: The built-in software that tells a device's hardware how to work.
glossary.share buybacks: When a company uses money to buy its own shares from investors.
glossary.MCP: Model Context Protocol: a standard way for AI apps to connect to outside tools.
glossary.2FA: Two-factor authentication: a sign-in check that asks for a second proof of identity as well as a password.
glossary.CDP: Chrome DevTools Protocol: a way for software to control or inspect a browser.
glossary.reaction vector: A list showing how much each substance is used up or produced in one reaction.
glossary.stoichiometric subspace: The set of changes in substance amounts you can get by combining the network’s reaction changes.
glossary.equilibrium: A state where the amounts of the substances stop changing.
glossary.rate constant: A number in the model that describes how fast a reaction happens.
glossary.deficiency zero theorem: A result that uses the way reactions are connected to limit how many points with unchanging concentrations a system can have.
glossary.clipper: Software that replaces a copied or pasted cryptocurrency address with an attacker's address.
glossary.card skimmer: Code that captures payment card details entered on a website and sends them to someone else.
glossary.Optimizely bundle: A package of website code from Optimizely that a site loads to run experiments.
glossary.squircle: A shape between a square and a circle, with rounded corners.
glossary.superellipse: A family of curves that can look rounder or squarer depending on a number.
glossary.Bézier curve: A smooth bend made by setting points that guide its shape.
glossary.curvature: How sharply a line or curve bends at a point.
glossary.gauge: In this article, a measurement based on where the curve crosses the midpoint of a quadrant.
glossary.G2 continuity: A way of joining curve sections so their direction and how sharply they bend both change smoothly at the join.
